x:
Elephants live in close family groups called herds, and each herd is usually led by the oldest female, known as the matriarch. She remembers where to find water during dry seasons, which paths are safe, and how to react when danger is near. Her daughters, granddaughters, and their young stay with her for most of their lives, while young males leave the herd when they are teenagers.

Elephants communicate in surprising ways. Besides trumpeting, they make low rumbles that are too deep for human ears to hear. These sounds can travel for miles, and other elephants may even sense the vibrations through their feet.

An elephant's trunk is just as remarkable. It contains tens of thousands of muscles, and it is strong enough to lift a log but gentle enough to pick up a single peanut. Elephants use their trunks to breathe, smell, drink, greet each other, and comfort a calf that is upset.

Most bats hunt at night, but they don't rely only on their eyes to find food. Instead, many of them use a skill called echolocation. A bat sends out a stream of high-pitched calls, and then it listens for the echoes that bounce back from objects nearby. By measuring how long each echo takes to return, the bat can tell how far away something is, how big it is, and even which way it's moving.

This system is so precise that some bats can detect an object as thin as a human hair. It lets them zoom through dark caves and forests without crashing, and it helps them catch insects in midair.

Bats are far more helpful than many people realize. A single little brown bat can eat hundreds of mosquitoes and other insects in an hour. Other bats pollinate flowers or spread seeds, and plants such as the agave and some kinds of bananas depend on them.

Monday, August 7

Today was my first day helping Mrs. Alvarez with her beehives, and I was more nervous than I expected. She gave me a white suit, gloves, and a veil, and then she showed me how to use a smoker. A few gentle puffs of smoke calm the bees, so they are less likely to sting.

When she lifted the first frame out of the hive, it was covered with thousands of bees. Most of them were workers, which are all female. Some were feeding the young, some were building wax cells, and others were coming home with yellow pollen on their legs. She pointed out the queen, who was longer than the others and was surrounded by a circle of helpers.

The most amazing thing I saw was a bee doing a waggle dance. Mrs. Alvarez explained that the dance tells the other bees which direction to fly and how far away the flowers are. I watched it three times, and I still can't believe insects can share directions like that.

When people think of penguins, they often picture ice and snow, but not every penguin lives in a frozen world. Nearly all of the world's penguin species live in the Southern Hemisphere, and they are found on the coasts of South America, Africa, Australia, and New Zealand, as well as in Antarctica. The Galapagos penguin even lives close to the equator, where it cools off in chilly ocean currents.

Emperor penguins, the largest species, have one of the hardest jobs in the animal kingdom. During the dark Antarctic winter, the female lays a single egg and then goes to sea to feed. The male balances the egg on his feet and covers it with a warm fold of skin. For about two months, he stands in the freezing wind with thousands of other males, and they huddle together and take turns moving to the warm center of the group.

When the chick hatches, the mother returns, and the parents take turns caring for it.

t: Newton's Laws at the Skate Park
x:
More than 300 years ago, Isaac Newton described three laws of motion, and you can see all of them at a skate park. The first law says that an object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion keeps moving, unless a force acts on it. That's why a skateboard keeps rolling after you push off, but it eventually slows down because of friction with the ground and the air.

The second law explains that the more force you use, the faster an object speeds up, and heavier objects need more force to get moving. A light push sends an empty skateboard rolling quickly, but the same push barely moves a board with a rider on it.

The third law says that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. When a skater kicks backward against the ground, the ground pushes the skater forward. The same idea explains how rockets launch, how swimmers move through water, and why a balloon zooms across the room when you let the air out.

Baking is really a series of chemical reactions that happen in your kitchen. Take pancakes, for example. Many recipes call for baking soda, which is a base. When it mixes with an acid, such as buttermilk or lemon juice, it produces tiny bubbles of carbon dioxide gas. Those bubbles get trapped in the batter, and they make the pancakes light and fluffy.

Bread works in a different way. Instead of baking soda, most bread uses yeast, which is a living organism. When the dough rests in a warm place, the yeast eats sugars in the flour and gives off carbon dioxide, so the dough slowly rises. The heat of the oven then makes the gas expand even more before the bread sets.

Heat also causes browning. When the surface of a cookie or a loaf of bread gets hot, sugars and proteins react with each other, and they create the golden color and rich smell that make baked goods so tempting. Next time you bake, you'll know that you're also doing science.

For our science lab last week, my partner Tyler and I built a density tower. We wanted to see whether liquids with different densities would stack on top of each other without mixing. We used honey, dish soap, water with blue food coloring, vegetable oil, and rubbing alcohol with a drop of red coloring.

We poured each liquid slowly down the side of a tall glass jar, starting with the heaviest. The honey sank straight to the bottom, and the dish soap formed a thick layer above it. The blue water settled on top of the soap, but some of it mixed in at first, so we had to wait a few minutes. Then the oil floated above the water, and the alcohol made a thin red layer at the very top.

Afterward, we dropped small objects into the jar. A grape stopped in the water layer, a bolt sank to the honey, and a piece of cork floated on top. Our results showed that an object sinks until it reaches a liquid that is denser than it is, and I thought that was the coolest part of the whole lab.

Sunlight looks white, but it is actually made of every color of the rainbow mixed together. Each color travels as a wave, and the waves have different lengths. Red light has the longest waves, while blue and violet light have much shorter ones.

When sunlight enters Earth's atmosphere, it runs into countless tiny molecules of gas. These molecules scatter short waves of light far more than long waves, so blue light gets bounced all over the sky. No matter which direction you look during the day, some of that scattered blue light reaches your eyes. Violet light scatters even more, but our eyes are less sensitive to it, and some of it is absorbed high in the atmosphere, so the sky looks blue to us.

At sunrise and sunset, the light has to travel through much more air to reach you. By then, most of the blue has been scattered away, and the reds, oranges, and pinks are left. That's why the sky seems to glow with warm colors at the beginning and end of the day.

On July 16, 1969, a giant Saturn V rocket lifted off from Florida carrying three astronauts: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins. Their mission, Apollo 11, had a goal that once seemed impossible. They were going to land on the Moon and return safely to Earth.

Four days later, Armstrong and Aldrin climbed into the lunar module, which was named the Eagle, and they separated from the main spacecraft. Collins stayed behind and orbited the Moon alone. As the Eagle descended, Armstrong saw that the planned landing spot was covered with boulders, so he took control and flew to a safer place. They touched down in an area called the Sea of Tranquility with very little fuel to spare.

A few hours later, Armstrong stepped onto the dusty surface. Hundreds of millions of people watched on television as he said, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." The astronauts collected rocks, set up experiments, and planted a flag before they began their journey home.

Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system, and it is so big that more than 1,000 Earths could fit inside it. Unlike Earth, it has no solid surface to stand on. It is made mostly of hydrogen and helium, and its colorful stripes are bands of clouds that race around the planet in opposite directions.

One of Jupiter's best-known features is the Great Red Spot. It is a giant storm, wider than Earth, and astronomers have watched it swirl for more than 300 years. Even though it has been shrinking over the past century, it is still the largest known storm in the solar system.

Jupiter also has dozens of moons. In 1610, the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei pointed his telescope at the planet and discovered its four largest moons, which are now called Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. Io has active volcanoes, and Europa may hide an ocean of liquid water beneath its icy crust. Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, and it is even bigger than the planet Mercury.

Last Saturday, our astronomy club took a trip to an observatory in the mountains. We left right after lunch and arrived just before sunset, and the air was so cold that I was glad I had packed my thickest jacket. Once it was dark, the sky was filled with more stars than I had ever seen. Without the lights of the city, I could even see the faint band of the Milky Way stretching overhead.

The observatory had a huge telescope inside a dome that rotated. A volunteer named Dr. Patel explained that the roof opens like a slot, so the telescope can point at any part of the sky. First, she showed us Saturn. When it was my turn, I gasped, because I could clearly see its rings and even a tiny dot that she said was its moon Titan.

Then we looked at a cluster of stars and a glowing cloud of gas where new stars are forming. By the time we got back on the bus, it was after midnight. I was tired, but I couldn't stop thinking about how huge the universe is.

Light is the fastest thing in the universe. It travels about 186,000 miles per second, which is fast enough to circle Earth more than seven times in one second. Even so, the distances in space are so enormous that light still takes time to reach us.

Light from the Moon reaches Earth in a little more than one second, and light from the Sun takes about eight minutes. That means when you see the Sun, you're seeing it as it was eight minutes ago. Stars are much farther away, so astronomers measure their distances in light-years. A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, nearly six trillion miles.

This creates a fascinating effect. When we look at a star that is 100 light-years away, we see light that left it a century ago. Powerful telescopes can detect galaxies so distant that their light has traveled for billions of years. In a way, every telescope is also a time machine, because it shows us what the universe looked like long ago.

In 1912, a German scientist named Alfred Wegener noticed something odd about maps. The coasts of South America and Africa looked like they could fit together like pieces of a puzzle. He also found similar fossils and rocks on continents separated by wide oceans. Wegener suggested that the continents had once been joined in a single giant landmass, which he called Pangaea, and that they had slowly drifted apart.

At first, many scientists rejected his idea, because he couldn't explain what made the continents move. Decades later, researchers mapping the ocean floor found long underwater mountain ranges where new crust was forming. Their discoveries led to the theory of plate tectonics.

Today, we know that Earth's outer layer is broken into large plates that float on hotter, softer rock below. They move only a few centimeters each year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Over millions of years, though, that slow motion builds mountains, opens oceans, and causes earthquakes and volcanoes along the edges of the plates.

Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, but they are home to about a quarter of all ocean species. Although they look like rocks or plants, reefs are built by tiny animals called coral polyps. Each polyp builds a hard skeleton of limestone around its soft body, and over hundreds of years, millions of these skeletons pile up to form a reef.

Most reef-building corals have a partnership with tiny algae that live inside their tissues. The algae use sunlight to make food, and they share some of it with the coral. In return, the coral gives the algae a safe place to live. The algae also give many corals their bright colors.

The largest reef system in the world is the Great Barrier Reef, which stretches for more than 1,400 miles off the northeast coast of Australia. It is so large that astronauts can see it from space. Scientists study reefs closely, because when the water becomes too warm, corals can lose their algae and turn white, and the whole reef community is affected.

Last night, a thunderstorm rolled across our town, and my younger brother Eli was too nervous to sleep. I sat with him on the back porch, where we were safely under the roof, and I taught him a trick that our grandfather taught me.

"When you see a flash of lightning," I said, "start counting the seconds until you hear the thunder." Lightning and thunder happen at the same moment, but light travels almost instantly, while sound moves much more slowly. It takes sound about five seconds to travel one mile. So if you count to ten, the lightning was about two miles away.

The first flash lit up the whole yard, and Eli counted to fifteen before the rumble arrived. "Three miles," he said proudly. As the storm got closer, the numbers got smaller, so we went inside to stay safe. We kept counting from the kitchen window, and by the time the storm moved off to the east, Eli was yawning and had forgotten that he was ever scared.

Many of the world's largest caves were carved out by water. It starts when rain falls through the air and seeps into the soil. Along the way, the water picks up carbon dioxide, which turns it into a weak acid. When that water trickles into cracks in limestone, it slowly dissolves the rock. Over hundreds of thousands of years, the tiny cracks grow into tunnels, rooms, and huge underground chambers.

Inside a cave, the dripping water can also build things. Each drop leaves behind a little bit of mineral as it falls from the ceiling. Over time, those minerals form stalactites, which hang down like icicles. The drops that land on the floor build stalagmites, which point upward. Sometimes the two meet in the middle and form a column.

The longest known cave system in the world is Mammoth Cave in Kentucky. Explorers have mapped more than 400 miles of its passages, and they think there is still more to discover.

The Silk Road wasn't a single road at all. It was a network of trade routes that linked China with Central Asia, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean world for well over a thousand years. Merchants rarely traveled the whole distance. Instead, goods passed from trader to trader, and they changed hands many times in busy market cities such as Samarkand.

The routes took their name from Chinese silk, a smooth, shiny fabric that was highly prized in Rome and other distant places. Traders also carried spices, tea, porcelain, glassware, horses, and precious stones. Caravans of camels crossed deserts and mountains, and travelers rested at roadside inns called caravanserais.

Ideas traveled along the Silk Road too. Papermaking spread west from China, while new foods, music, art, and languages moved in every direction. In the 1200s, a young merchant from Venice named Marco Polo journeyed to China, and his stories later helped Europeans imagine the lands far to the east.

In the early 1800s, moving goods from the Atlantic coast to the Great Lakes was slow and costly. Wagons had to cross rough roads and steep hills, and the trip could take weeks. So the governor of New York, DeWitt Clinton, pushed for a bold plan. He wanted to dig a canal across the state to connect the Hudson River with Lake Erie.

Many people laughed at the idea and called it "Clinton's Ditch." Construction began in 1817, and workers dug most of it by hand with shovels, picks, and help from horses and mules. Since the land was higher in the west, engineers built a series of locks, which raise and lower boats like water elevators.

When the canal opened in 1825, it stretched 363 miles from Albany to Buffalo. Shipping costs dropped sharply, and New York City grew into the country's busiest port. Towns along the canal, such as Rochester and Syracuse, grew quickly too, and the canal helped open the Midwest to farmers and settlers.

To my dear cousin Marcus,

Greetings from Rome! I arrived last week with my father, and I have never seen a city so crowded or so grand. More people live here than in any other city I've heard of, and the streets are full of merchants, soldiers, and travelers from every corner of the empire.

Yesterday, we walked through the Forum, which is the center of the city. There were temples, law courts, and speakers giving loud speeches to anyone who would listen. Then we visited the public baths. They have a hot pool, a warm pool, and a cold pool, and people go there to wash, exercise, and talk with their friends.

What amazes me most is the water. Huge stone channels called aqueducts carry fresh water into the city from springs that are miles away, and it flows into fountains on almost every street. Father says Roman engineers are the best in the world, and I believe him. I'll write again soon and tell you about the roads, which are paved with stone and seem to stretch forever.

Your cousin, Lucius

Benjamin Franklin is remembered as one of the founders of the United States, but he was also a printer, a writer, a scientist, and an inventor. He was born in Boston in 1706, and he left school when he was only ten years old. Even so, he loved to read, and he taught himself about science, history, and languages.

As a young man, Franklin moved to Philadelphia and opened his own printing shop. He published a newspaper and a popular yearly book called Poor Richard's Almanack, which was full of weather predictions, jokes, and wise sayings. He also helped start the city's first lending library and one of its first volunteer fire companies.

Franklin was fascinated by electricity. His experiments showed that lightning is a form of electricity, and they led him to invent the lightning rod, which protects buildings during storms. He later invented bifocal glasses and a stove that heated rooms more efficiently than an open fireplace. He never patented his inventions, because he wanted everyone to be able to use them.

Venice, Italy, is one of the most unusual cities in the world. It was built on a group of more than 100 small islands in a shallow lagoon, and instead of streets, it has canals. The islands are connected by hundreds of bridges, and there are no cars in the historic center at all. People walk or travel by boat, and even the buses, taxis, and ambulances float.

The largest waterway, the Grand Canal, curves through the middle of the city like a giant letter S. It is lined with old palaces, churches, and markets, and it has been one of the city's main highways for centuries. Visitors often ride in gondolas, which are long, narrow, black boats steered by a rower who stands at the back with a single oar.

Venice also faces a challenge. During very high tides, water can flood its squares and walkways, so the city built movable barriers that rise from the sea floor to hold back the water. Engineers and scientists continue to look for ways to protect this one-of-a-kind city.

The Sahara in northern Africa is the largest hot desert in the world. It covers about 3.6 million square miles, which makes it roughly the size of the United States. It stretches across all or part of more than ten countries, including Egypt, Libya, Algeria, Morocco, Mali, and Niger.

Many people picture the Sahara as an endless sea of sand dunes, but dunes cover only part of it. Much of the desert is made of rocky plateaus, gravel plains, dry valleys, and mountains. Some of its dunes, though, are taller than a 50-story building.

Life in the Sahara can be extreme. Daytime temperatures in summer often climb above 100 degrees Fahrenheit, but the nights can be surprisingly cold, because the dry air doesn't hold heat well. Even so, people have lived in and traveled across the desert for thousands of years. Oases, where underground water reaches the surface, support palm trees, gardens, and towns. Camels, which can go for days without drinking, are still used to carry people and goods across the sand.

Before the late 1800s, most towns set their clocks by the Sun. When the Sun was highest in the sky, it was noon. This worked fine when people traveled by horse, but it became confusing once trains could cross many towns in a single day. Each town had its own time, so train schedules were a mess.

In 1883, American and Canadian railroads adopted a system of standard time zones, and a year later, an international meeting chose the line through Greenwich, England, as the starting point for measuring longitude and time. The idea is simple. Earth spins once every 24 hours, so the world can be divided into 24 zones, each about 15 degrees of longitude wide. As you travel east, the clock usually moves ahead one hour for each zone you cross.

In the middle of the Pacific Ocean, there is a line called the International Date Line. When you cross it heading west, you skip ahead one day, and when you cross it heading east, you go back a day. That means it can be Tuesday on one side and Monday on the other.

On the third day of our trip to Morocco, my mom and I explored the markets of Marrakech. The old part of the city is surrounded by thick red walls, and inside them, there is a maze of narrow, winding alleys called souks. Each section seemed to sell something different, and I quickly lost track of where we were.

In one alley, shopkeepers sold spices piled in colorful mounds, and the air smelled of ginger, cinnamon, and mint. In another, there were rows of leather bags, brass lamps, and handwoven rugs in every pattern you can imagine. A man showed us how he hammered designs into metal plates, and he let me try it. My design was crooked, but he smiled and said it was very good for a beginner.

That evening, we went to the city's huge main square. It was filled with food stalls, musicians, and storytellers, and the smoke from the grills drifted over the crowd. We drank sweet mint tea and watched the sun set behind the Atlas Mountains. It was the best day of the whole trip.

Every year, my grandmother hosts Thanksgiving dinner for our entire family, and that means twenty-two people squeezed into her house. This year, she decided I was old enough to join what she calls the kitchen crew, so I arrived at seven in the morning with my apron and a lot of nervous energy.

My first job was peeling potatoes, and there were more of them than I could count. Then my cousin Diego and I chopped celery and onions for the stuffing while my aunt made the cranberry sauce from scratch. Grandma was in charge of the turkey, and she checked on it every half hour like it was a baby.

Things didn't go perfectly. I accidentally added sugar instead of salt to the mashed potatoes, and we had to start that batch over. However, by three o'clock, the table was covered with food, and everyone was gathered around it. Before we ate, Grandma thanked the kitchen crew by name. I've never been so tired, but I've also never been so proud of a bowl of potatoes.

When I turned thirteen, my parents started giving me a weekly allowance of fifteen dollars. At first, I spent it as soon as I got it. I bought snacks after school, games for my phone, and things I didn't really need, so by the middle of the week, I usually had nothing left.

Then I decided I wanted a new pair of running shoes, and they cost ninety dollars. My dad suggested that I try a simple budget. Every week, I put five dollars into a jar for savings, set aside three dollars to give to a local animal shelter, and kept the rest to spend. I also wrote down everything I bought in a small notebook.

Keeping track was eye-opening. I realized that I was spending more on snacks than on anything else, so I started bringing them from home. It took me about four months, but I finally bought the shoes with my own money. Now I'm saving for a bike, and I feel much more in control than I did before.

t: How to Study for a Big Test
x:
A big test can feel overwhelming, but a good plan makes it much easier. Here are some strategies that really work.

First, start early. Cramming the night before might help you remember facts for a few hours, but your brain learns better when you study in short sessions spread over several days. Try reviewing for twenty or thirty minutes a day for a week instead of studying for three hours at once.

Next, test yourself instead of just rereading your notes. Make flash cards, answer the practice questions at the end of each chapter, or explain the topic out loud to a friend or family member. If you can teach it, you probably understand it.

Find a quiet place to work, and put your phone in another room so it won't distract you. Take short breaks, drink water, and eat a healthy snack. Finally, get plenty of sleep, especially the night before the test. Your brain sorts and stores what you learned while you sleep, so rest is part of studying too.

Dear Grandpa,

Thank you so much for the birthday card and the old fishing tackle box. Mom told me it was the same one you used when you were my age, so I'll take good care of it. I already put my hooks, lures, and extra line inside it.

School has been busy this fall. I'm taking a coding class, and last week, we built a simple game where a cat has to catch falling fish. I thought you'd like that, since you're the one who taught me to fish in the first place. I'm also on the cross-country team, and at our last meet, I finished in eleventh place out of forty runners, which was my best time yet.

I can't wait to visit you at the lake this summer. Could we try fishing at sunrise again, like we did last year? I still remember how calm and quiet the water was, and how we saw a heron standing in the reeds. Please tell Grandma that I miss her cooking, especially her blueberry pancakes.

Love, Owen

The first recorded Olympic Games took place in 776 BC in Olympia, a site in southern Greece. At first, there was only one event, a short footrace of about 200 yards. Over time, the Greeks added longer races, wrestling, boxing, chariot races, and the pentathlon, which combined running, jumping, wrestling, and throwing the discus and the javelin.

The games were held every four years, and athletes traveled from all over the Greek world to compete. Winners didn't receive gold medals. Instead, they were crowned with wreaths made from olive branches, and they returned home as heroes.

The ancient games ended many centuries later, but they weren't forgotten. In the 1890s, a French educator named Pierre de Coubertin worked to bring them back, and the first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens in 1896. About 240 athletes from 14 countries competed. Today, thousands of athletes from more than 200 nations take part, and the Winter Games, which began in 1924, include sports such as skiing, skating, and hockey.

A good pitcher can make a baseball curve on its way to home plate, and the batter may swing at a ball that seems to drop or dart away at the last moment. This isn't magic. It's physics, and the secret is spin.

When a pitcher throws a curveball, they flick their wrist so that the ball spins quickly as it leaves their hand. As the spinning ball flies forward, its raised red seams grab the air around it. On one side of the ball, the spin moves in the same direction as the passing air, and on the other side, it moves against it. This difference changes how the air flows around the ball, and it creates a force that pushes the ball sideways or down. Scientists call this the Magnus effect.

The same effect explains how soccer players bend a free kick around a wall of defenders and how tennis players use topspin to make the ball dip over the net. The faster the ball spins, the more it curves, so practice and a strong wrist make a big difference.

It was the bottom of the ninth inning, and our team was losing by one run. There were two outs, a runner was on second base, and it was my turn to bat. As I walked to the plate, I could hear my teammates cheering, but my hands were shaking so much that I could barely hold the bat.

The first pitch was a fastball, and I swung too late. Strike one. The second pitch was low and outside, so I let it go. Then I stepped out of the batter's box and took a deep breath, just as Coach Romero had taught us. "Watch the ball, and keep your swing short," I told myself.

The next pitch came straight down the middle. I swung, and I felt the solid crack of the bat before I even saw where the ball went. It flew over the shortstop's glove and bounced into left field. The runner on second raced around third and slid home just ahead of the throw. We had tied the game, and when Jasmine hit a double two pitches later, I ran home with the winning run.

For my thirteenth birthday, my aunt took me to an indoor climbing gym. I had always wanted to try rock climbing, but when I saw the walls, which were almost forty feet tall, my stomach did a flip.

Before we started, an instructor named Kayla taught us the basics. She showed us how to put on our harnesses, tie a figure-eight knot, and check each other's gear. She explained that a partner on the ground, called the belayer, holds the rope and catches you if you slip. "Use your legs more than your arms," she said, "because your legs are much stronger."

My first attempt didn't go well. I grabbed the holds too tightly, and my arms got tired halfway up, so I let go and swung gently back down. On my second try, I followed Kayla's advice, pushed with my legs, and took my time choosing each hold. When I finally slapped the top of the wall, I looked down and saw my aunt cheering below. Since then, I've climbed every weekend, and I'm already working on harder routes.

William Shakespeare is one of the most famous writers in the English language, and many of his plays were first performed at the Globe Theatre in London. The Globe was built in 1599 near the south bank of the River Thames. It was a round, open-air building with three levels of seats and a stage that stuck out into the yard.

Going to a play at the Globe was a lively experience. The cheapest tickets cost a penny, and those audience members, called groundlings, stood in the yard right in front of the stage. Wealthier people paid more to sit in the covered galleries. There was no electric lighting, so plays were performed in the afternoon, and crowds often cheered, booed, and talked back to the actors.

In 1613, a cannon fired during a performance set the thatched roof on fire, and the theater burned down. Luckily, no one was hurt, and the Globe was rebuilt the next year. Centuries later, a careful reconstruction opened in 1997 close to the original site, and today, visitors can watch Shakespeare's plays there just as audiences did 400 years ago.

A haiku is a very short poem that began in Japan. In English, haiku are often written in three lines, with five syllables in the first line, seven in the second, and five in the third. Many haiku describe a single moment in nature, and they often mention a season, such as the first snow of winter or a frog jumping into a pond.

One of the most famous haiku poets was Matsuo Basho, who lived in Japan in the 1600s. He traveled across the country on foot, and he wrote about the mountains, rivers, and people he saw along the way. His poems are simple, but they are full of feeling.

Writing your own haiku is a good way to practice paying attention. First, go outside, or look out a window, and notice something small, like a leaf, a bird, or a puddle. Then describe it with clear, specific words instead of explaining how you feel. Count the syllables carefully, and don't be afraid to rewrite. A haiku is short, but choosing the right words can take time.

My friends and I started a band last spring. Mateo plays the drums, Hannah plays the bass, and I play guitar and sing. For months, we practiced in Mateo's garage every Tuesday and Friday, and his neighbors were very patient with us.

In October, the school announced a talent show, and we decided to enter. We chose two songs, one that we wrote ourselves and one that we had loved for years. The week before the show, we practiced every single night. On the night of the show, though, I was so nervous that I almost forgot the words to the first verse.

When the curtain opened, the lights were brighter than I expected, and I couldn't see the audience at all. Mateo counted us in, and as soon as we started playing, my nerves disappeared. Halfway through our second song, Hannah's bass string broke, but she kept playing on the other three strings, and nobody even noticed. When we finished, the crowd clapped and cheered so loudly that we just stood there grinning. We didn't win first place, but we've already started writing our next song.

Making a bowl from clay takes patience, but the steps are easier than you might think. Here's how our art teacher, Ms. Okafor, taught us to do it with the pinch method.

First, take a lump of clay about the size of a tennis ball, and knead it on the table for a few minutes. This pushes out air bubbles, which can cause the bowl to crack later. Then roll the clay into a smooth ball between your palms.

Next, press your thumb into the center of the ball, but don't push all the way through. Hold the ball in one hand, and gently pinch the walls between your thumb and fingers as you turn it. Work your way around and up, little by little, until the walls are even and about as thick as a pencil.

When you're happy with the shape, smooth the rim with a damp sponge, and carve your initials on the bottom. Let the bowl dry slowly for about a week. After that, it gets fired in a very hot oven called a kiln, and then you can paint it with glaze and fire it a second time to make it shiny.

Thomas Edison is one of the best-known inventors in American history. In 1876, he built a laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey, and he filled it with tools, chemicals, and a team of skilled workers. He wanted the lab to produce a new invention about every ten days, and some people called it an invention factory.

In 1877, Edison and his team built the phonograph, a machine that could record sound and play it back. The first words Edison recorded were from the nursery rhyme "Mary Had a Little Lamb." People were amazed, and newspapers began calling him the Wizard of Menlo Park.

Edison didn't invent the first electric light, but he worked hard to make one that was practical and long-lasting. His team tested thousands of materials for the thin thread inside the bulb, and in 1879, they found one that glowed for many hours. Edison then helped design power stations and wires to bring electricity into homes and businesses. By the end of his life, he held more than 1,000 patents in the United States.

Whenever a phone or car shows your position on a map, it's probably using the Global Positioning System, or GPS. This system depends on about 30 satellites that circle Earth roughly 12,500 miles above the surface. They are arranged so that at least four of them are above the horizon almost anywhere on the planet.

Each satellite carries a very precise atomic clock, and it constantly sends out signals that say what time it is and where the satellite is. A GPS receiver, like the one in your phone, picks up these signals. Since the signals travel at the speed of light, the receiver can measure how long each one took to arrive, and then it figures out how far away each satellite is.

With the distance to one satellite, the receiver knows only that it is somewhere on a giant sphere. With three satellites, it can narrow its position down to a single point, and a fourth satellite helps correct small timing errors. The whole process takes just a few seconds, and it can find your location to within a few feet.

Alexander Graham Bell was born in Scotland in 1847, and he later moved to North America. His mother was deaf, and his father taught speech, so Bell grew up fascinated by sound and how people hear it. As a young man, he taught deaf students in Boston, and in his spare time, he experimented with ways to send sound through wires.

Bell worked with a skilled machinist named Thomas Watson, and together they built and tested many devices. In 1876, Bell received a patent for the telephone. A few days later, he spoke into his new invention while Watson waited in another room. According to Bell's notes, his first words were, "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you." Watson heard him clearly and came running.

At first, some people thought the telephone was just a toy. Within a few years, however, telephone lines were being built in cities across the United States and Europe. Bell also went on to work on other inventions, including early flying machines and devices that sent sound using beams of light.

People have used tools to help them calculate for thousands of years. One of the earliest was the abacus, a frame with rows of beads that slide back and forth. Merchants in ancient China, Rome, and other places used it to add, subtract, and keep track of their goods.

In the 1830s, an English mathematician named Charles Babbage designed a machine that he called the Analytical Engine. It was meant to follow instructions punched into cards, and his friend Ada Lovelace wrote what many people consider the first computer program for it. The machine was never finished, but their ideas were far ahead of their time.

The first electronic computers appeared in the 1940s. One of them, called ENIAC, filled a large room and weighed about 30 tons. It used thousands of glass tubes that often burned out. Later, inventors replaced those tubes with tiny parts called transistors, and then they learned to place millions of transistors on a single chip of silicon. Today, a laptop or phone is far more powerful than ENIAC, and it fits in your backpack or your pocket.
